tips.title: El and la: every noun is masculine or feminine
body: Every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine, and "the" changes to match: el for masculine, la for feminine.
Words ending in -o are usually masculine and words ending in -a usually feminine, but learn each noun with its el or la.

tips.title: No need for "he", "she" or "I"
body: The verb ending already tells you who is doing it, so Spanish usually leaves out the subject.
Es mi hermano means "he is my brother", and tengo means "I have". You only add él, ella or yo for emphasis.

tips.title: Adjectives go after the noun and match it
body: Describing words usually come after the noun: la casa blanca, "the white house".
They also match the noun: pequeño becomes pequeña for a feminine noun, and both add -s in the plural. Adjectives ending in -e, like grande, stay the same for both.

tips.title: Tengo hambre: Spanish "has" hunger
body: Where English says "I am hungry", Spanish says "I have hunger": tengo hambre. The same goes for being sleepy, thirsty, cold or a certain age.
So use tener, not ser or estar, for these.

tips.title: Quiero + a verb: "I want to…"
body: To say you want to do something, put the verb in its dictionary form (ending in -ar, -er or -ir) right after quiero.
To say no, put no in front of the verb: no quiero.

tips.title: Gustar works backwards
body: Me gusta literally means "it pleases me". The thing you like is the subject, so the verb matches it: gusta for one thing, gustan for several.
Me is "to me", te is "to you". The thing liked takes el or la, even when English drops "the".

tips.title: Asking questions
body: Written questions open with an upside-down ¿ and close with ?, so you know from the start that it's a question.
Question words always carry an accent: qué, quién, dónde, cómo, cuánto, por qué. The answer "because" is porque, one word with no accent.

tips.title: Estar for where things are
body: Spanish has two verbs for "to be". Use estar to say where something is: el libro está en la mesa.
En covers both "in" and "on". De + el contracts to del: debajo del sofá.

tips.title: Telling someone what to do
body: To give a friendly instruction, use the "he / she" form of the present tense: gira (turn), sigue (keep going), mira (look).
It works for anyone you'd call tú.

tips.title: Ser or estar?
body: Ser is for what someone or something is: job, origin, personality. Estar is for states and location: how you feel, where you are, and married or single.
Soy profesora (my job), estoy bien (how I am right now), estoy casado (married).

tips.title: Usted: the polite "you"
body: With shop staff, strangers and older people, use usted. It takes the same verb form as "he / she": ¿tiene otra talla? (do you have another size?).
With friends and family, use tú: ¿tienes?

tips.title: Quisiera: a softer "I want"
body: Quiero is fine with friends, but ordering with quisiera ("I would like") sounds more polite.
Para mí, … ("for me, …") is another natural way to order.

tips.title: Me levanto: verbs you do to yourself
body: Some verbs take me, te or se because you do them to yourself: levantarse (to get up), ducharse (to shower), vestirse (to get dressed).
The little word goes before the verb: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta.

tips.title: The past: what happened (preterite)
body: For a finished action in the past, use the preterite. Regular -ar verbs end in -é for "I" (hablé), and -er / -ir verbs in -í (comí).
Ir (to go) and ser (to be) share the same past forms: fui means both "I went" and "I was".

tips.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event
body: Spanish uses the imperfect to set the scene: what was going on, what used to happen (vivía, caminaba). It uses the preterite for the event that happened (encontró).
Think of the imperfect as the background and the preterite as the action.

tips.title: Had done: había + -ado / -ido
body: To say something had already happened before another past event, use había plus the past participle: se había ido (he had left).
Mientras (while) usually takes the imperfect for the longer action.

tips.title: Plans: voy a + verb, and si + present
body: Voy a + a verb is the everyday future: voy a reservar (I'm going to book).
With si (if) about a real possibility, use the present on both sides: si llueve, nos quedamos (if it rains, we'll stay).

tips.title: Me duele: pain works like gustar
body: Me duele means "it hurts me": the body part is the subject, with el or la instead of "my". For two body parts, use duelen.
Desde (since) with the present says how long something has been going on: tengo fiebre desde ayer.

tips.title: Giving advice: deberías, yo que tú, and the subjunctive
body: Deberías + verb is "you should". Yo que tú ("if I were you") takes the conditional: iría, diría.
After phrases like te recomiendo que or es importante que, the next verb goes into the subjunctive, which swaps the vowel of the ending: duermes becomes duermas, tomas becomes tomes.

tips.title: Fue cancelado: the passive
body: To say what was done to something, use ser + the past participle, which matches the noun: el vuelo fue cancelado, la reunión fue cancelada.
In conversation, people often use se instead: se canceló el vuelo.

tips.title: Creo que… / No creo que…
body: Creo que (I think that) is followed by the normal present: creo que tienes razón.
But when you doubt or deny it, use the subjunctive: no creo que sea justo (I don't think it's fair).

tips.title: Aunque: "although" or "even if"
body: Aunque + the normal present states a fact: aunque es difícil (although it is hard).
Aunque + the subjunctive makes it hypothetical or concedes the point: aunque sea difícil, vale la pena (even if it's hard, it's worth it).

tips.title: Tú or usted?
body: Usted is for people you don't know, older people, customers and formal situations. Tú is for friends, family and people your age.
In Colombia usted is also used warmly between friends and family, so you'll hear it everywhere. When unsure, start with usted and switch if the other person asks: ¿nos podemos tutear?

tips.title: Extra-polite requests
body: The conditional (podría, sería, agradecería) softens any request.
Le agradecería que is followed by the past subjunctive: que me respondiera (that you replied).

tips.title: Culture: dating in Colombia
body: Meeting through friends, at a party or a dance class is very common, and a first plan is often a group outing before a one-on-one date.
Compliments are warm and frequent: linda (lovely) and bonito (nice) are everyday words, and a kind "¡Qué detalle!" is the gracious way to take one.
Social plans often start late ("la hora colombiana"), but if you've agreed on a time for a coffee date, being on time is appreciated.

tips.title: Culture: texting in Colombia
body: Almost everyone texts on WhatsApp, and voice notes are just as common as written messages.
"¿Qué más?" is the classic Colombian hello. Laughter is "jajaja", and "tqm" (te quiero mucho) goes to friends and partners alike.
Getting "left on read" is "dejar en visto". "Cuadrar" means to set up a plan.

tips.title: Culture: meeting the family
body: Family matters a lot, and meeting your partner's family can happen fairly early, often at a Sunday lunch.
Use usted with your partner's parents until they tell you to use tú, and bring something small: dessert, pastries or flowers.
Offering to help clear the table always goes down well.

tips.title: Culture: compliments in Colombia
body: Warm compliments are part of everyday conversation, and a well-placed "¡qué linda sonrisa!" in a friendly chat comes across as charming.
A piropo shouted at a stranger in the street is a different thing: many people find it rude or intimidating, and it's best left out.
Compliment something specific (their laugh, their style, their taste in music) and watch how they respond before going further.

tips.title: Culture: teasing (mamar gallo)
body: Colombians love playful teasing, called mamar gallo. Light, friendly jokes and a quick comeback are a big part of flirting.
Keep it about small things (who won the game, who's the better dancer), never someone's looks or anything they might be sensitive about.
Cheesy pick-up lines work best said with a grin, as a joke you're both in on.

tips.title: Culture: being clear and kind
body: Being direct about liking someone is fine, and asking for their number is normal. A "no" or a vague answer should be taken gracefully.
If you misread the situation, a simple apology and a friendly exit ("fue un gusto charlar contigo") leaves everyone comfortable.
Good-morning messages like "¿cómo amaneciste?" are a sweet, common way to show interest by text.

tips.title: Culture: greetings in Spain and Latin America
body: Spain: two kisses on the cheek (right, then left) when women meet anyone; men usually shake hands with each other. Colombia, Mexico and most of Latin America: one kiss on the right cheek. In Argentina, men who are friends kiss on the cheek too.
Always greet when you walk into a small shop, a lift or a waiting room: "¡Buenos días!" or just "¡Buenas!". Asking for something without greeting first sounds cold.
In Colombia, usted is warm, not just formal: many people use it with friends and family. In Spain, tú comes quickly, even with strangers your age.
Gestures: Colombians often point with their lips. In Mexico and Colombia, show a person's height with your hand sideways; a flat palm facing down is for animals.

tips.title: Culture: meals in Spain and Latin America
body: Spain eats late: lunch around 2 to 4 p.m. and dinner from 9 p.m. In Colombia and Mexico lunch, around noon to 2, is the big meal (the "menú del día" or "corrientazo" is a cheap set lunch), and dinner is lighter, around 7.
The waiter won't bring the check until you ask for it: lingering is normal. Say "¡Buen provecho!" to people who are eating, even other diners as you walk out.
Tips: in Colombia the bill often asks "¿Desea incluir el servicio?", an optional 10%. In Mexico leave 10 to 15%; in Spain, rounding up is enough.
Food words change: juice is "jugo" in Latin America and "zumo" in Spain; potato is "papa" and "patata".

tips.title: Culture: holidays around the Spanish-speaking world
body: Spain: at midnight on New Year's Eve, people eat twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock, for luck. Children get presents from the Three Kings (los Reyes Magos) on January 6.

Colombia: December 7 is the Día de las Velitas, when families light candles and paper lanterns to start Christmas. From December 16 to 24, people gather for the novena. Many holidays move to a Monday, giving a "puente" (long weekend).
Mexico: on the Día de Muertos (November 1 and 2), families build an ofrenda with photos, marigolds and pan de muerto to remember their loved ones. It's a warm celebration of memory, not Halloween.

tips.title: Culture: mistakes foreigners make
body: False friends: "embarazada" means pregnant, not embarrassed. Say "qué vergüenza", or in Colombia "qué pena". In Spain, "estoy constipado" means you have a cold.
"Ahorita" can mean now, soon or not today. Social plans often start late, but work meetings start on time.
In Latin America everyone from the Americas is "americano", so call someone from the US "estadounidense".
In Spain "coger" simply means to take or catch, but in much of Latin America it's vulgar: say "tomar" or "agarrar" (agarrar el bus).

tips.title: Culture: one language, many slangs
body: "Cool" is chévere in Colombia and Venezuela, guay in Spain, padre or chido in Mexico and copado in Argentina.
"Buddy" is parce or parcero in Colombia, tío or tía in Spain and güey in Mexico (very casual). In Argentina, "che" is how you call out to a friend.
"Vale" for OK marks you as someone who learned in Spain. Latin Americans say "listo" (Colombia), "sale" (Mexico) or "dale" (Argentina, Colombia).
Slang is for friends: keep it out of job interviews and emails to your boss.
